overview: Influenza (flu) is a highly contagious acute respiratory illness caused by influenza A, B, C, or D viruses. It infects the nose, throat, and sometimes the lungs. Unlike the common cold, flu symptoms appear suddenly and are significantly more severe. There are around 1 billion cases of seasonal influenza globally each year, including 3–5 million severe cases and up to 650,000 respiratory deaths. Annual vaccination is the most effective preventive measure.

types.name: Influenza Type A
types.description: The most severe type. Infects both humans and animals (birds, pigs, horses). Classified by hemagglutinin (H1–H16) and neuraminidase (N1–N9) subtypes. Responsible for all major pandemics (e.g., H1N1, H3N2).

types.name: Influenza Type B
types.description: Milder than Type A. Infects primarily humans. Not subdivided into subtypes but has two main lineages (Yamagata and Victoria). Responsible for seasonal epidemics.

types.name: Influenza Type C
types.description: Causes very mild respiratory illness, usually in children. Rarely leads to epidemics and is not included in seasonal flu vaccines.

types.name: Influenza Type D
types.description: Primarily affects cattle. Not known to infect or cause illness in humans currently.

types.name: Pandemic Influenza
types.description: Occurs when a new influenza A virus emerges with significant antigenic changes (antigenic shift), against which most humans have little or no immunity. Major pandemics include the 1918 Spanish flu, 1957 Asian flu, 1968 Hong Kong flu, and 2009 H1N1 pandemic.

symptoms: Intense muscle aches and joint pain
Vomiting and diarrhea (more common in children)
causes: Influenza A virus — most common cause of severe seasonal and pandemic flu
Influenza B virus — causes seasonal flu epidemics, mainly in humans
Inhalation of respiratory droplets from an infected person (talking, coughing, sneezing)
Touching surfaces or objects contaminated with influenza virus, then touching mouth, nose, or eyes
Antigenic drift — gradual mutations causing seasonal flu strains to evade prior immunity
Antigenic shift — sudden major genetic change creating a new pandemic strain
risk_factors: Age 65 years and above (weakened immune response)
Pregnant women (especially in second and third trimester)
Chronic medical conditions: asthma, COPD, diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease
Immunocompromised individuals (HIV/AIDS, cancer treatment, organ transplant)
Residents of nursing homes or long-term care facilities
Healthcare workers with frequent exposure to sick patients
diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis — sudden onset of fever, cough, and muscle aches suggests flu
Rapid Influenza Diagnostic Tests (RIDTs) — results in 10–15 minutes, moderate sensitivity
Rapid Molecular Assays (PCR-based) — high sensitivity and specificity, results in ~20 minutes
Viral culture — gold standard for confirmation, takes 3–10 days; used in surveillance
Direct and indirect immunofluorescence assays (DFA/IFA) — lab-based detection
Chest X-ray — if pneumonia is suspected
Blood tests — CBC may show leukopenia (low white cell count) typical of viral infections

antiviral_drugs: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — oral capsules/liquid; most widely used; most effective if started within 48 hours
Zanamivir (Relenza) — inhaled; alternative to oseltamivir; not for people with breathing problems
Baloxavir Marboxil (Xofluza) — single oral dose; newer mechanism targeting RNA polymerase
Peramivir (Rapivab) — IV form for hospitalised patients unable to take oral medication
symptomatic_relief: Paracetamol or Ibuprofen — for fever and body aches
Cough suppressants and decongestants — for nasal and cough symptoms
Saline nasal rinse — for nasal congestion
home_care: Rest completely until fever-free for at least 24 hours without medication
Drink plenty of fluids — water, clear soups, electrolyte drinks
Stay home and avoid contact with others to prevent spread
Use a separate room and bathroom if possible during illness
severe_cases: Hospitalisation with IV fluids and oxygen therapy
Treatment of complications (secondary bacterial pneumonia with antibiotics)

complications: Secondary bacterial pneumonia (most common serious complication)
Worsening of chronic diseases (asthma attacks, COPD exacerbation, heart failure)
Encephalitis or Reye's syndrome (rare, especially in children given aspirin)
prevention: Annual flu vaccination — most important preventive measure; updated each year to match circulating strains
Inactivated Influenza Vaccine (IIV) — injection; suitable for all age groups including pregnant women
Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine (LAIV) — nasal spray; for healthy non-pregnant individuals 2–49 years
Wash hands frequently with soap and water for 20+ seconds
Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
Cover mouth and nose with elbow or tissue when coughing or sneezing
Avoid close contact with sick people
Stay home when sick to prevent spreading infection
Disinfect frequently touched surfaces — phones, keyboards, door handles
Maintain healthy habits — adequate sleep, balanced diet, regular exercise
emergency_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath at rest
Inability to stay awake or be roused
Severe or persistent vomiting — unable to keep fluids down
Signs of dehydration — no urination for 8+ hours, dry mouth, sunken eyes
Symptoms improve then return with fever and worsening cough (secondary infection)

faqs.question: Why do I need a flu vaccine every year?
faqs.answer: Influenza viruses mutate continuously through a process called antigenic drift. Each year, the circulating strains change. The WHO monitors global flu activity and updates vaccine composition annually to match the most likely circulating strains, so last year's vaccine may not be effective against this year's viruses.

faqs.question: How is flu different from the common cold?
faqs.answer: Flu symptoms appear suddenly and are much more severe — high fever, intense muscle aches, chills, and extreme fatigue are hallmarks. Cold symptoms develop gradually and mainly affect the nose and throat. Flu also carries a significantly higher risk of serious complications.

faqs.question: When should I take antiviral medication for flu?
faqs.answer: Antivirals like oseltamivir (Tamiflu) are most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. They reduce illness duration and severity. They are particularly recommended for high-risk individuals (elderly, pregnant, with chronic conditions) and hospitalised patients.

faqs.question: Can I get flu from the flu vaccine?
faqs.answer: No. The injected flu vaccine (IIV) contains inactivated (killed) virus and cannot cause flu. Some people experience mild soreness, redness at the injection site, or a low-grade fever — these are normal immune responses and not the flu itself. The nasal spray (LAIV) contains live weakened virus but cannot cause flu in healthy individuals.
